issues.legal_issue: Industries requiring operating consent must keep primary effluent treatment plants functional, and defaulting industries may be restrained from operating.
material_facts: The petition sought directions requiring industries that need operating consent to have functional effluent treatment plants.

The parties did not dispute that industries requiring operating consent had primary effluent treatment plants when consent was granted, but the continuing functionality of those plants after operations began was in issue.

The Court directed notice to the relevant industries, inspections after the notice period, and restraint of industrial activity where a plant was not made fully operational; electricity could be disconnected on the Pollution Control Board's recommendation.
issues.conclusion: Pollution Control Boards must give the specified notice, inspect the relevant industries, and restrain any industry whose primary effluent treatment plant is not functional; the electricity agency must disconnect supply when the Board recommends disconnection for that reason.
issues.legal_principle: An industry that requires operating consent may operate only while its primary effluent treatment plant is functional. The Court relied on that condition for operation and issued directions to secure compliance; it cited no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this direction.

issues.legal_issue: An industry restrained because its primary effluent treatment plant is non-functional may resume industrial activity only after restoring the plant and obtaining fresh operating consent.
material_facts: The Court directed that an industry disabled from carrying on industrial activity could make its primary effluent treatment plant functional to the required capacity and seek fresh operating consent.
The Court specified that industrial activity could resume only after fresh consent was received.
issues.conclusion: A restrained industry may resume industrial activity only after its primary effluent treatment plant is functional to the required capacity and it receives fresh operating consent.
issues.legal_principle: Operation requires both a functional primary effluent treatment plant and operating consent from the relevant Pollution Control Board. The Court cited no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this direction.

issues.legal_issue: Pollution Control Boards must verify complaints of industrial non-compliance and take legally permissible action against verified defaulters.
material_facts: The Court granted private individuals and organizations liberty to complain to the relevant Pollution Control Board about an industry's default.
The Court directed the Board to verify complaints and, if default was established, take action permitted by law, in addition to discontinuing industrial activity as directed.
issues.conclusion: A Pollution Control Board receiving a complaint must verify it and, if the alleged default is confirmed, take legally permissible action, including the directed discontinuation of industrial activity where applicable.
issues.legal_principle: Complaints of non-compliance must be verified before action is taken, and the Board may take action permissible in law in addition to the specified operational restraint. The Court cited no earlier cases or specific statutory provision for this direction.

issues.legal_issue: Common effluent treatment plants must be completed urgently, with unstarted plants completed within the prescribed implementation period and additional land acquired for possible future zero-liquid-discharge plants.
material_facts: The Court was informed that the central government, state governments or union territories, and industrial areas or clusters were expected to contribute to financing common effluent treatment plants.
Some common plants were already under implementation, while others had yet to be set up; setting up a plant could require financing and land acquisition.
The Court directed completion of plants already under implementation within their existing timelines and completion of plants yet to be set up within the period it specified.
The Court also directed acquisition of additional land for zero-liquid-discharge plants if needed in the future.
issues.conclusion: Common effluent treatment plants already under implementation should be completed within their existing timelines; those not yet set up must be completed within the period directed, and additional land must be acquired for possible future zero-liquid-discharge plants.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the establishment of common treatment infrastructure as an urgent environmental measure and directed state governments and union territories to implement it, including planning for future treatment needs. No earlier cases or specific statutory provision were cited for these directions.

issues.legal_issue: Municipalities and local bodies bear responsibility for operating existing common effluent treatment plants and may raise funds from beneficiaries; state governments or union territories must meet operating costs if funding norms are not timely established.
material_facts: Some existing common effluent treatment plants were dysfunctional because of inadequate finances or unrepaired damage linked to lack of funds.

The Court identified municipal responsibilities under Article 243W of the Constitution and item 6 of the Twelfth Schedule concerning public health, sanitation, conservancy, and solid-waste management.

The Court held that municipalities or local bodies were responsible for operating existing common plants and could devise norms to recover funds from commercial, industrial, and domestic beneficiaries.

The process for devising funding norms was to be supervised by the relevant state government or union territory; if norms were not in place before the next financial year began, the state government or union territory had to meet the financial requirements from its own resources.
The Court referred to Articles 243X and 243Y as a means of addressing financial constraints.
issues.conclusion: Municipalities and local bodies must operate existing common effluent treatment plants and may raise funds from facility beneficiaries under supervised funding norms; if those norms are not timely in place, the relevant state government or union territory must fund the dysfunctional plants' operating needs from its own resources.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 243W and item 6 of the Twelfth Schedule, municipalities have responsibilities relating to public health, sanitation, conservancy, and solid-waste management, supporting their duty to operate existing common treatment plants. Articles 243X and 243Y provide a means to address financial constraints. No earlier cases were cited.

issues.legal_issue: Sewage treatment plants must also be established and made functional under the implementation framework applied to common effluent treatment plants.
material_facts: The Court considered sewage treatment alongside the measures for common effluent treatment plants.
It directed that sewage treatment plants be set up and made functional within the timelines and in the format laid down for the common treatment plant directions.
issues.conclusion: Sewage treatment plants must be set up and made functional under the same implementation timelines and framework directed for common effluent treatment plants.
issues.legal_principle: The Court directed simultaneous treatment of sewage and industrial effluent through the same implementation framework. No earlier cases or specific statutory provision were cited for this direction.

issues.definition: When sewage requires treatment and treatment infrastructure is needed, public authorities must establish and operate sewage treatment plants under the applicable implementation framework.

issues.legal_issue: Specified public officials and environmental authorities must monitor and implement treatment-plant directions, maintain and transmit data, and provide a forum for complaints about non-implementation.
material_facts: The Court stated that directions would be ineffective without a rigid implementation mechanism.
It assigned implementation responsibilities to Pollution Control Board Member Secretaries and made the relevant state or union-territory Environment Department Secretary answerable for default.
It directed government secretaries to monitor progress, issue directions to Pollution Control Boards, and collect and maintain data.
The data was to be provided to the Central Ground Water Authority for evaluation and onward submission to the relevant National Green Tribunal bench.

The relevant Tribunal benches were directed to maintain periodically listed files for complaints; Pollution Control Boards were directed to initiate legally permissible civil or criminal action against defaulters.
Private individuals and organizations were permitted to approach the relevant Tribunal bench about deficiencies in implementation.
issues.conclusion: The identified officials and authorities must implement, monitor, and document compliance; the Central Ground Water Authority must evaluate and transmit the data; the relevant Tribunal benches must supervise implementation complaints; and Pollution Control Boards must pursue legally permissible action against defaulters.
issues.legal_principle: The Court required an accountable monitoring and enforcement mechanism, including data collection, evaluation, Tribunal supervision, and legally permissible action. No earlier cases or specific statutory provisions were cited for these directions.

issues.legal_issue: Earlier court or Tribunal timelines that expire sooner, and any longer timeline already provided, are not displaced by the newly directed timelines.
material_facts: The Court clarified that its directions and timelines would not dilute earlier court or National Green Tribunal directions where the existing timeline expired sooner.
It also clarified that the new timelines would apply only where there was no existing timeline or where a longer period had already been provided.
issues.conclusion: The new timelines do not extend or dilute an earlier, sooner-expiring timeline, and apply only where no existing timeline applies or a longer period has been provided.
issues.legal_principle: The Court expressly preserved prior court and Tribunal directions with earlier-expiring timelines and limited its new timelines to the stated circumstances. No earlier cases beyond the existing directions themselves were identified.

issues.legal_issue: State governments and union territories must establish online, real-time continuous systems that publicly display emission levels.
material_facts: The Court considered public access to environmental monitoring information important to implementing its directions.
It was informed that some state governments had already adopted online, real-time continuous monitoring measures.

The Court directed all relevant state governments and union territories to put such systems in place within the period it specified, displaying emission levels on the relevant Pollution Control Board portal.
issues.conclusion: Each state government and union territory must establish an online, real-time continuous monitoring system that displays emission levels publicly on the relevant Pollution Control Board portal.
issues.legal_principle: The Court considered public-domain, continuous emission monitoring an implementation measure for environmental compliance. No earlier cases or specific statutory provisions were cited for this direction.
